conversation.content:
Good morning—I’m so glad you’re here. My name is Maya Bennett, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’ll be guiding you through a short screening called the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale—EPDS for short. It’s simply a 10-question check-in about how you’ve been feeling in the past seven days since your baby arrived. There are no right or wrong answers, and everything we discuss stays between us unless safety is a concern. My goal is to understand how you’re coping so we can make sure you get the support you deserve.

We’ll take it one gentle question at a time, and you can answer in your own words. Ready to begin?

To start: In the past week, how often have you felt able to laugh and see the funny side of things, even when life with a new baby feels chaotic?

Honestly, it’s been hard. I used to laugh so easily—my husband and I would joke around all the time—but lately I barely crack a smile. Maybe once or twice I’ve managed a quick laugh when something silly happened with the baby, but it fades fast. Most of the time I’m just too tired and tense to find anything funny.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Not very often. Maybe once or twice the whole week—like when the baby let out a huge burp and my husband and I both cracked up—but the moment passes fast and I’m right back to feeling flat.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Not really. I used to get excited about little things—coffee with a friend, a walk, even just a quiet shower—but this week nothing feels worth looking forward to. When I think about plans, I just feel tired and wonder if I’ll even enjoy them, so mostly I don’t bother.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… a lot. If the baby’s fussy, I immediately think it’s because I’m not doing something right—maybe I ate the wrong thing, or I’m not holding him the way he needs. When he wouldn’t nap yesterday I kept replaying everything I’d done, convinced it was my fault. I know in my head that babies just cry, but I still feel like I’m failing him somehow.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Pretty much every day. I’ll be feeding him and suddenly my heart’s racing because I’m sure he’s not breathing right, even though he’s perfectly fine. Or I’ll lie down and worry the crib’s too cold, too hot, too soft… I check the monitor a dozen times a night. Nothing “bad” has actually happened, but I can’t shake the fear that something will.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Yes, it hits me out of nowhere. A couple of nights this week I’d be changing her diaper and suddenly feel like the walls were closing in—heart pounding, chest tight, can’t catch my breath. It passes after a few minutes, but there’s no real trigger; it just shows up and leaves me shaky.
Things have been getting on top of me

Most days. It feels like the minute I finish one feeding, the next is already due, laundry’s piled up, and I’m running on empty. Sometimes I just sit on the couch with the baby in my arms, staring at the mess, thinking I’ll never dig my way out. I manage the basics, but it’s like I’m drowning in small stuff that never used to bother me.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Yeah… I lie down exhausted, but my head won’t stop spinning—did I burp her enough, is the onesie too tight, am I already failing her tomorrow? I toss and turn for an hour or more, then wake up every time I hear a squeak on the monitor. Even when the baby’s sleeping, I can’t stay asleep.
I have felt sad or miserable

That’s most of my day. I wake up feeling heavy, like there’s a weight on my chest. I’ll look at her little face and feel love, but it’s clouded by this gray sadness I can’t shake. It’s not constant sobbing—just this dull ache that sits with me from morning to night.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

A few times this week. Yesterday I set the baby in the crib for two seconds and she started shrieking; I just burst into tears, sank onto the floor, and couldn’t stop. It’s usually those small, ordinary moments that tip me over—never anything huge, just the feeling that I can’t handle even the tiniest hiccup.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No—never. I’m tired and overwhelmed, but I would never want to hurt myself. I just want to feel better so I can be the mom she deserves.

You've shared that the past week has felt heavy and gray-laughter comes rarely, plans feel pointless, and even small tasks leave you feeling underwater. Despite loving your baby, you carry a constant ache, frequent tears, and waves of panic or self-blame that strike out of nowhere. You are exhausted yet unable to rest, and you long to feel like yourself again so you can fully enjoy motherhood.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 24, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports only rare moments of laughter (once or twice all week) and a quick return to flat mood, aligning with "Definitely not so much now"</sym>, <sym>Patient expresses a near-complete loss of anticipatory pleasure, describing a week where "nothing feels worth looking forward to" and avoiding plans, matching "Hardly at all".</sym>, <sym>Patient reports frequent, intense self-blame ("a lot," "immediately think it's because I'm not doing something right," "convinced it was my fault") matching "Yes, most of the time."</sym>, <sym>Patient reports daily, intrusive, unfounded worries about infant safety, consistent with 'very often</sym>, <sym>Patient describes sudden, intense panic attacks with physical symptoms occurring multiple times in the past week without triggers, matching "Yes, quite a lot"</sym>, <sym>She reports feeling overwhelmed "most days" and "drowning in small stuff," matching "sometimes I haven't been coping as well as usual."</sym>, <sym>Patient describes nightly inability to fall or stay asleep due to racing worries about motherhood, matching 'Yes, most of the time</sym>, <sym>The patient describes pervasive sadness that fills "most of my day," matching the highest-severity option.</sym>, <sym>The patient reports crying multiple times this week, indicating frequent unhappiness consistent with "Yes, quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** With an EPDS of 24 (well above the ≥14 threshold), your endorsement of core symptoms-<sym>depressed mood</sym> most of the day, marked <sym>loss of interest</sym>, <sym>guilt</sym>, <sym>sleep disruption</sym>, <sym>tearfulness</sym>, and recurrent <sym>panic-like episodes</sym>-aligns with <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>. Item 10 was denied, indicating no current self-harm ideation. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent appointment with your <med>obstetrician</med>, <med>primary-care provider</med>, or a <med>perinatal mental-health specialist</med>
2. Ask about evidence-based treatments such as <med>CBT</med>, peer support groups, or <med>antidepressant medication</med> compatible with breastfeeding
3. Plan small, manageable daily goals-5-minute shower, 10-minute outdoor walk, accepting help with chores-to reduce overwhelm
4. Practice 4-7-8 breathing or grounding exercises when <sym>panic</sym> arises; keep a written reminder on your phone
5. Share these results with a trusted partner, friend, or family member so they can assist with night shifts, meals, or appointments
6. Schedule a follow-up EPDS in two weeks to monitor progress after starting support or treatment
7. If distress escalates or self-harm thoughts emerge, contact the 24/7 <med>National Maternal Mental Health Hotline</med> (1-833-943-5746) or local emergency services
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 24: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Date: [today]  

Presenting symptoms (self-report):  
- Persistent low mood, described as “gray sadness” most of the day  
- Marked anhedonia (no pleasure in previously enjoyed activities)  
- Daily tearfulness; two episodes of spontaneous, prolonged crying  
- Sleep disturbance (initial insomnia, frequent nocturnal awakenings) unrelated to infant needs  
- Excessive, irrational guilt about parenting adequacy (“blaming myself… feel like I’m failing him”)  
- Recurrent, intrusive worries about infant safety without objective basis  
- Sudden panic-like episodes (tight chest, dyspnoea, racing heart) occurring multiple times this week  
- Sense of being “drowning in small stuff,” difficulty completing daily tasks  

Pattern: Symptoms present “most days” for the past week, interfering with functioning; no self-harm ideation reported.

Screening significance:  
High endorsement of items consistent with probable major depressive episode with peripartum onset and comorbid anxiety symptoms; no current suicidal ideation.

Risk factors identified:  
- Depressed mood, anhedonia, guilt, sleep loss, frequent crying  
- Daily anxiety and panic symptoms  
- Subjective sense of impaired coping / being overwhelmed  
- Denies any thoughts of self-harm (documented safety factor)

Next steps: Recommend formal clinical assessment (diagnostic interview, PHQ-9/EPDS scoring) and same-day discussion of support, psycho-education, and treatment options.
